claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a well-defined hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale secondary phases and heterointerfaces in a predominantly solid-solution matrix.

A reduced-parameter model explicitly incorporating the hierarchical heterostructure can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior more rapidly and accurately than traditional first-principles or full multiscale simulations.
Equilibrium elastic constants and misfit volumes are suitable reduced inputs for analytical alloy-strengthening models.
Interfacial characteristics of the HfNbTiVAl10 hierarchy can be represented by reduced parameters in the proposed model.
The hierarchical heterostructure acts as a barrier to dislocation motion and thereby modulates yield strength.
The hierarchical heterostructure blunts cracks and thereby affects fracture behavior.
The hierarchical heterostructure influences the overall elastic response of HfNbTiVAl10.
Nanostructured interfaces and precipitate distributions filter the active deformation mechanisms.
Hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates can enhance dislocation accumulation and storage, strain hardening, and ductility.
Solid-solution and interface effects produce predictable changes in yield behavior.
The hierarchical structure improves resistance to crack propagation.
Explicit DFT evaluation of alloy yield strength and fracture is generally beyond the reach of available implementations.
Brute-force first-principles and detailed molecular-dynamics simulations are slower and less adaptable to heterogeneous multiscale effects than the proposed model.
The proposed model will reduce computational time by roughly a factor of ten.
The proposed model will predict Young’s modulus and yield strength with errors near or below 10%.
The proposed model will provide improved predictions of fracture initiation and propagation.
The model may fail when thermal processing, extreme temperature, or severe plastic deformation alters the hierarchical heterostructure.
The model may fail when oxidation-induced phases or interstitial effects dominate the mechanical response.
Young’s modulus can be measured from the slope of the linear-elastic region of a tensile stress-strain curve, although alignment, deformation measurement, and data analysis can introduce error.
A prediction error greater than 20%, or failure to reproduce trends with temperature and microstructural homogenization, is declared to decisively falsify the hypothesis.
